title: Yagi beams, gain and matching
blurb: Explain Yagi element roles, what raises gain and bandwidth, the dBi and dBd scales, and how hairpin and gamma matches work.

G9C01.why: **Larger-diameter elements** widen the SWR bandwidth. Thin elements make the match sharper and narrower.
G9C01.trap: Closer spacing and loading coils don't widen it.

G9C02.why: The driven element is about **½ wavelength**, like a dipole.

G9C03.why: The **reflector is longer** than the driven element and the **directors are shorter**.
G9C03.trap: Don't swap them: short elements in front, long behind.

G9C04.why: A dipole is already 2.15 dBi, so the same antenna reads **2.15 dB higher in dBi**.

G9C05.why: More directors on a longer boom **increase gain** and narrow the beam.

G9C07.why: Front-to-back ratio is the **main-lobe power compared with the power radiated the opposite way**.

G9C08.why: The main lobe is the **direction of maximum radiated field strength**.

G9C09.why: Two stacked Yagis give about twice the power: 10 log 2 ≈ **3 dB**.

G9C10.why: **Boom length, number of elements and element spacing** can all be adjusted to trade gain, front-to-back and SWR bandwidth.

G9C11.why: A hairpin (beta) match is a **shorted stub at the feed point** of the Yagi.
G9C11.trap: A quarter-wave 75 Ω section is a different matching trick.

G9C12.why: A gamma match **doesn't need the driven element insulated from the boom**.
